items.followUp: State two conclusions Rutherford drew from the alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: Identifies that most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that most alpha particles passed through the foil (with or without saying they were undeflected).

rubric.why: Identifies the deflection or backward scattering of a small number of alpha particles.
rubric.description: A small number were deflected; a very small number bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing deflection or backward scattering of a small number of alpha particles.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.
A few alpha particles were deflected, and a very small number bounced back.

items.followUp: What was Mendeleev’s contribution to the classification of elements?

rubric.why: Recognises Mendeleev as a Russian chemist.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying him as a Russian chemist.

rubric.why: States his role in arranging elements according to atomic mass or formulating the periodic law.
rubric.description: He arranged elements in a periodic table in order of increasing atomic mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing his periodic table or classification based on atomic mass.

modelAnswer: Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist.
He arranged the elements in a periodic table in order of increasing atomic masses.

items.followUp: Name the two series that make up the f-block of the periodic table.

rubric.why: Locates the f-block in the detached rows beneath the main body of the periodic table.
rubric.description: The f-block is shown in two separate rows at the bottom of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly locating the f-block below the main body of the table.

rubric.why: Identifies the two series in the f-block.
rubric.description: The two rows are the lanthanide and actinide series.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both series.

modelAnswer: The f-block is shown as two separate rows at the bottom of the periodic table.
These rows are the lanthanide and actinide series.

items.followUp: Write the names and symbols of the Group II elements.

rubric.why: Gives correct names and symbols for Group I elements.
rubric.description: Correctly names and gives symbols for at least four Group I elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for four correct name-symbol pairs from Group I.

rubric.why: Completes the Group I list with the remaining heavier elements.
rubric.description: Correctly names and gives symbols for the remaining Group I elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the remaining correct name-symbol pairs; accept either spelling of caesium.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen (H), lithium (Li), sodium (Na), and potassium (K) are Group I elements.
Rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs), and francium (Fr) are also Group I elements.

items.followUp: Define ionization energy and give one example.

rubric.why: Defines electron affinity as the energy change when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron.
rubric.description: Electron affinity is the energy released when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition, including an atom accepting an electron and energy being released.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of an atom accepting an electron.
rubric.description: For example, Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻ + energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example showing an atom gaining an electron to form a negative ion.

modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
For example: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻ + energy.

items.followUp: Name four types of chemical bond and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Names two of the four principal types of chemical bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both ionic and covalent bonds.

rubric.why: Names the other two types of chemical bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both coordinate covalent (dative covalent) and metallic bonds.

modelAnswer: The four types of chemical bond are ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent, and metallic bonds.

items.followUp: Identify the types of covalent bonds in N₂ and H₂.

rubric.why: Identifies the carbon-carbon bond in ethyne as a triple covalent bond.
rubric.description: C₂H₂ has a triple covalent bond between its two carbon atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the C–C bond as triple.

rubric.why: Identifies the C–H bonds in methane as single covalent bonds.
rubric.description: CH₄ has single covalent bonds between carbon and hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the bonds in methane as single.

modelAnswer: C₂H₂: the two carbon atoms are joined by a triple covalent bond.
CH₄: carbon and hydrogen atoms are joined by single covalent bonds.

items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?

rubric.why: Explains that oppositely charged ions in an ionic compound are held together by strong electrostatic forces.
rubric.description: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction act between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the strong attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Connects the strong ionic attractions to the large energy needed to separate ions.
rubric.description: A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces, so ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that substantial energy is required to overcome the ionic attractions.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
A large amount of energy is required to overcome these forces, so ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.
